en: The Sūtra on the Parinirvāṇa of King Śuddhodana, translated by the Song dynasty layman Juqu Jingsheng.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with...
Together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One’s radiance was brilliant, like the rising sun illuminating the world.

Then, the King of the Śākyas, named Śuddhodana—who ruled by the True Dharma, honored propriety, virtue, benevolence, and righteousness, and constantly practiced a compassionate heart—was afflicted by a grave illness. The four elements within his body simultaneously became disordered, ravaging his physical frame; his limbs and joints felt as if they were coming apart, and his breathing was unstable, like the rushing flow of a torrential stream.

The prime minister issued a proclamation throughout the kingdom for all skilled physicians to assemble. They examined the King’s ailment and administered various medicines according to the disease, employing every kind of treatment, yet none were able to cure him. As the auspicious signs of his end had already arrived, he would soon die.
At that time, the king was restless and agitated, tossing and turning without ceasing like a fish in shallow water.
When the queen and the court ladies saw him in such a state, their grief and distress increased all the more.
At that time, King Śuklodana, King Droṇodana, King Mahānāman, and all the ministers raised their voices together, saying:
"If the King should now pass away, we shall forever lose his protection, and the kingdom will fall into weakness."
The king’s body trembled, his lips and mouth grew parched, his voice repeatedly faltered, and tears fell from his dazzled eyes.
At that time, all the kings, with reverent hearts, knelt long upon their knees with palms joined and spoke together:

“By nature, Great King, you have not been fond of doing evil; in the mere twinkling of an eye, you have accumulated merit without satiety. You protect and nourish the people so that none fail to find peace, and your fame resounds throughout the ten directions.”
"Great King, for what reason are you so distressed today?
At that moment, King Śuddhodana’s voice emerged as he addressed the kings, saying:

"Though my life is coming to an end, I do not consider it a hardship; I only regret that I shall not see my son Siddhārtha, nor my second son Nanda, who would have eliminated greed, lust, and all worldly desires."
Furthermore, he lamented not seeing Ānanda, the son of Droṇodana, who upholds the treasury of the Buddha’s Dharma without losing a single word;
and he also lamented not seeing his grandson Rāhula, who, though young in years, possesses complete supernormal powers and flawless observance of the precepts.
"If I were able to see these sons of mine, though my illness be grave and I have not yet escaped birth and death, I would not consider it a hardship.
When those standing by the king heard these words, there was none who did not weep, their tears falling like rain.
At that time, King Śuklodana replied to King Śuddhodana, saying:
"I have heard that the World-Honored One is at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha, which is fifty yojanas distant from here."
Your Majesty is now increasingly frail; were you to dispatch a messenger, the road would be so vast and remote that I fear it would arrive too late to be of any benefit.
I only pray that Your Majesty will not be so deeply distressed or preoccupied with anxious thoughts for your sons.
At that time, having heard these words, King Śuddhodana shed tears and replied to King Śuklodana:
"Although my sons are far away, my hope for them remains undiminished."

Why is this so? Because my son has attained Buddhahood and, through great compassion, constantly employs his supernormal powers—such as the celestial eye that sees clearly and the celestial ear that hears penetratingly—to rescue and receive those among sentient beings who are ready for deliverance. It is as if there were hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings drowning in water; with a heart of loving-kindness and pity, he provides them with boats and rafts to ferry them across to liberation, never becoming weary or exhausted.

It is, for example, like a person surrounded by bandits or encountering an enemy, who, in his panic and loss of wits, has no hope of self-rescue and seeks only protection and refuge, relying on one of power and influence, desiring liberation from that peril;
or like a person afflicted with a grave illness, who desires to find a skilled physician to treat his malady;
my beholding the World-Honored One today is likewise so.

Why is this so? Because throughout the day and night, at the three periods of time, the World-Honored One constantly uses his divine eye to observe those sentient beings who are ready to receive transformation, regarding them with a heart of compassion and pity, just as a mother thinks of her child.

At that time, the World-Honored One was on Vulture Peak Mountain. With his divine ear, he heard from afar the words of the royal father in the great city of Kapilavastu, who was filled with longing, as well as the words of the other kings. He then used his divine eye to see from afar that the royal father lay ill upon his bed, emaciated, exhausted, and haggard, his life about to reach its end. He knew that the father, thirsting and yearning, desired to see his sons.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Nanda, saying:
"King Śuddhodana, the Victorious King of the World, is our father.
He has now fallen gravely ill; we ought to go and see him. His remaining life is short, so prepare yourselves quickly and set forth at once."
"We should go while our lives still remain, so that we may meet with him and fulfill the King's wish.
Having received these instructions, Nanda knelt down and paid homage, saying:
"So be it, World-Honored One!"

"King Śuddhodana is our father; his deeds were extraordinary, for he was able to give birth to a holy son who brings benefit to the world. We should now go to him to repay the kindness of his nurturing."
Ānanda joined his palms, stepped forward, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I have longed to see you, O World-Honored One.
King Śuddhodana is my paternal uncle; he permitted me to leave the household life to become a disciple of the Buddha and take the Buddha as my teacher. For this reason, I wish to go.”
Rāhula again stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Although the World-Honored One is my father, he abandoned his kingdom to seek the Way. I was nurtured and brought to maturity by my grandfather-king before being permitted to leave the household life; therefore, I wish to go and pay my respects to my grandfather-king."
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent!
You should know that this is the right time; let the king's wish be fulfilled."
Thereupon, by means of his supernormal power, the World-Honored One leaped into the air like a king of geese and suddenly appeared in Kapilavastu, emitting a great radiance.
When the people of the kingdom saw the Buddha approaching from afar, they all raised their voices together and spoke with tears:
"If the Great King passes away, the name of the Śākyan kingdom will surely perish."
The people of the city wept before the Buddha and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"At that time, the Prince went beyond the palace walls and sat beneath a Lumbinī tree to engage in contemplation; when the King, his father, saw him, he bowed his head in respectful salutation."
"Great King, your life will thus soon come to an end; we pray that the Tathāgata would deign to go there at this time so that you may meet him.

The people of the kingdom rolled upon the ground, prostrating themselves, sobbing and weeping; among them were those who tore off their own necklaces, those who rent their garments, those who plucked out their hair, and those who took up ashes and dust to smear themselves, their pain piercing to the very marrow of their bones like that of madmen.
Having seen this, the Buddha admonished the people of the kingdom:
"Impermanence and separation have existed thus from antiquity to the present. You all!..."
"You should reflect upon this: birth and death are suffering; only the Way is true.
The Buddha then showered the hearts of sentient beings with the rain of Dharma, liberating them through various teachings.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One emitted a great radiance by means of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
he further emitted a great radiance by means of the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics;
and he emitted a great radiance by means of the merits cultivated throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
The light shone brilliantly, penetrating both inside and out, pervading the entire kingdom.
When the light illuminated the king’s body, his suffering and pain were relieved.
The king then spoke in wonder: "What light is this?"
"Is this the light of the sun and moon, or the light of the various devas?
This light has touched my body like celestial sandalwood, causing the afflictions and pains within my body to subside.
I am struck with wonder and suspicion; could it be that my son Siddhārtha has come? That he first manifested this radiance must surely be an auspicious omen!"
At that time, King Mahāyaśas entered the palace from outside and said to the Great King:
"The World-Honored One has arrived, leading his disciples Ānanda, Nanda, Rāhula, and others, coming through the air. Your Majesty should rejoice and cast off this heart of sorrow and anguish."
When the king heard that the Buddha had arrived, his heart leaped with reverence, and he rose from his seat unconsciously.
In a mere moment, the Buddha entered the palace.
Seeing the Buddha arrive, the king raised both hands from afar, clasped the Buddha’s feet, and spoke:
“I only pray that the Tathāgata will touch my body with his hand so that I may find peace.
I am oppressed by illness as if sesame seeds were being pressed for oil; the pain is unbearable, and my life is about to depart. How could I possibly return?”
"Now that I have finally been able to see the World-Honored One, my grief and resentment are immediately dispelled.
The Buddha, knowing that the King, his father, was gravely ill and emaciated, his complexion altered beyond recognition, and his physical form withered and unsightly to behold, [observed him].
The Buddha told Nanda:
"Observe how the King’s physical form was once majestic and his countenance upright; his fame resounded afar. Now that he has contracted a grave illness, he can no longer be recognized.
Where now are his handsome features and his reputation for valor and strength?"
At that time, King Śuddhodana, with single-minded devotion and palms joined, praised the World-Honored One, saying:
"Your vows have been fulfilled, and you have likewise satisfied the aspirations of sentient beings.
I am now afflicted by a grave illness; I pray that the Buddha will deliver me from this calamity."
You have magnificently adorned the lineage of Gautama; you are truly most extraordinary.
In this final age, you proclaim the True Dharma, acting as a protector for those who are without protection.
As a Dharma King, you drench and nourish all sentient beings with the flavor of the Dharma.
Thus, in future generations, my son shall be supremely compassionate and filial.
A jewel among men, his fame shall reach throughout the great trichiliocosm, extending upward even to the Śuddhāvāsa heavens;
he shall walk alone, without equal or peer.
The Buddha said, "I only pray that the King, my father, will no longer be sorrowful or distressed!
For what reason? Because..."
"His moral conduct is perfectly complete, without any deficiency.
The Buddha extended his golden arm from within his *kāṣāya*, its palm like a lotus flower, and placed his hand upon the forehead of the King:

"The King is a person of purity and virtuous discipline; the defilements of the mind have already been left behind. You should now rejoice and find delight; it is not fitting for you to be distressed."
You should contemplate with earnest attention the meaning of the various sūtras and dharmas; having planted roots of goodness, you shall attain a firm resolve where there was previously no stability.
Therefore, Great King, you ought to rejoice;
though your life is about to end, you may set your mind at ease.
At that time, King Mahāpraśasta, with a mind of deep reverence, addressed King Śuddhodana, saying:
"The Buddha was a prince who was fully endowed with supernatural powers, such that none could equal him;
his younger brother Nanda was also a prince who has already crossed the ocean of birth-and-death and all desires, remaining unimpeded throughout the four paths."

Ānanda, the son of King Droṇodana, has already tasted the flavor of the Dharma; regarding the teachings spoken by the Buddha, which are like a deep ocean, he does not forget a single phrase but retains them all through *dhāraṇī*.
Rāhula, the grandson of the King, is perfectly endowed with virtue and morality; having attained various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), he has realized the fruits of the four paths.
These four sons have already destroyed the net of Māra.

At that time, having heard these words, King Śuddhodana was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself; he immediately took the Buddha’s hand with his own and placed it upon his heart.
At his place of rest, the king looked up toward the World-Honored One with palms joined and addressed him, saying:
"I gaze upon the Tathāgata with unblinking eyes; I never tire of beholding you. My vows are fulfilled and my heart leaps with joy as I depart from you now."
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, brings great benefit; those who are able to see him or hear his teachings are all individuals possessed of marks and of great merit.
"Today the World-Honored One is my son; he has treated me with excessive kindness, and I have not been abandoned.

As the king joined his palms at his bedside and paid homage at the feet of the World-Honored One, the Buddha’s palm remained upon the king’s heart. Then, confronted by impermanence, his life ended and his breath ceased; suddenly, he passed away into the next world.

Thereupon, the Śākyas wailed and wept; they threw themselves to the ground, striking the earth with both hands, and loosening their topknots so their hair became disheveled, crying out with one voice:
"We have forever lost our protector!"

Among them, some tore off their own necklaces; some tore and ruined their own clothes; some took ash and dust to smear themselves; some pulled out all their hair; some spoke of how the King governed the country with righteousness and did not oppress the people;
and others said: "The various small kingdoms have lost their protection!"
"The King, the most honored among kings, has now passed away; the kingdom has lost its majesty and spiritual power.
At that time, the Śākyas bathed the king’s body with various fragrant liquids, wrapped it in karpāsa cotton and various silks, and placed it in a coffin.

They fashioned a lion throne adorned with the seven precious gems, draped with nets of pearls hanging around its sides, and then lifted the coffin and set it upon the lion throne, scattering flowers and burning incense.
The Buddha stood solemnly and respectfully before the head of the bier together with Nanda, while Ānanda and Rāhula remained at the feet.
Nanda knelt on his right knee and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“My father, the King, raised me; I pray that you will permit me, Nanda, to carry my father’s coffin.”
Ānanda joined his palms, stepped forward, and said to the Buddha,
“I only pray that you will permit me to carry my paternal uncle’s coffin.
Rāhula then stepped forward and said to the Buddha:
“May you graciously permit me to carry the coffin of my ancestral king.
At that time, the World-Honored One reflected upon future generations, when the people would become violent and fail to repay the kindness of their parents who raised them.

Because of this unfilial act, and for the sake of establishing the rites and laws for the sentient beings of the future, the Tathāgata personally desired to carry the coffin of his father, the King; immediately, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and all the mountains surged and subsided like boats upon the water.
At that time, all the devas of the desire realm, together with their countless hundreds of thousands of retinues, came together to attend the funeral.
Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King of the North, led hundreds of thousands of myriads of yakṣas and spirits to come together to attend the funeral;
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Heavenly King of the East, followed by hundreds of thousands of myriads of spirits of music and the like, came together to attend the funeral.
The Southern Heavenly King Virūḍhaka, accompanied by hundreds of thousands of millions of kumbhāṇḍa spirits and deities, came together to attend the funeral;

the Western Heavenly King Virūpākṣa, accompanied by hundreds of thousands of millions of nāga spirits and deities, also came together to attend the funeral, and they all joined in their lamentation, raising their voices in wailing and weeping.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings deliberated together in secret:

"Beholding the World-Honored One, for the sake of those in future generations who are unfilial toward their parents, he manifests his own person out of great compassion to carry the coffin of his royal father."
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings knelt together and, raising their voices in unison, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will allow us to carry the coffin of our father, the King."
Why is this so? We, too, are disciples of the Buddha;
we likewise have heard the Dharma from the Buddha and attained understanding, having obtained the purity of the Dharma-eye and realized the stage of Srotāpanna.
"For this reason, we ought to carry the coffin of our father, the King.
At that time, the World-Honored One permitted the Four Heavenly Kings to carry the coffin of the father king.

Then, the Four Heavenly Kings each transformed their bodies into human forms, supporting the coffin with their hands and bearing it upon their shoulders; all the people of the nation and the entire great assembly wept without exception.
At that time, the World-Honored One’s majestic radiance became even more manifest, as if ten thousand suns were shining together.
The Tathāgata personally took a censer in his hand and walked ahead of the funeral procession, proceeding to the burial site on Vulture Peak Mountain.
There were one thousand arhats who, by the power of their spiritual faculties, arrived traveling through the air; they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed him, saying:
“We pray only that the World-Honored One will command us as to what we should do!”
At that time, the Buddha addressed the arhats:
"Go quickly to the island in the great ocean and fetch various kinds of fragrant wood, such as ox-head sandalwood."

They immediately received the instruction and, in the time it takes to snap one's fingers, each arrived at the great ocean; together they gathered fragrant firewood, and in the time it takes to bend and extend the arm, they had already returned.
The Buddha, together with the great assembly, piled up fragrant wood and placed the coffin upon it, then set fire to it.
When the entire assembly saw the flames blazing fiercely, they all prostrated themselves before the Buddha, rolling on the ground in self-abasement, weeping even more piteously.
Those who had attained the Way all rejoiced in their own good fortune;
those who had not yet attained the Way felt their hearts tremble with fear, and the hair on their bodies stood on end.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the assembled multitude, saying:

“The world is entirely impermanent; it is suffering, empty, and not-self. It possesses no solidity; it is like an illusion, like a magical transformation, like a mirage in the heat, like the moon reflected in water; life does not endure for long.”
"You all! Do not see this fire and consider it merely hot; the fires of desire are far more intense than this.
Therefore, you should exhort yourselves to forever leave behind birth and death, for only then will you attain great peace."
When the fire had finished burning the Great King’s body, the various kings each took five hundred jars of milk to extinguish the flames.

Once the fire was extinguished, they vied with one another to collect the bones, placing them in golden caskets. They then immediately erected a stūpa over them, hanging silk banners, canopies, and various bells, making offerings to the shrine.
Then the great assembly simultaneously raised their voices and addressed the Buddha together, saying:
"The Great King Śuddhodana has now passed away; where has his spirit been reborn?
We only pray that the World-Honored One will analyze and explain this for us!"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly, saying:
"King Śuddhodana, my father, is a pure person; he has been reborn in the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven.
Upon hearing these words, the assembly cast off their grief and anguish.

When the Buddha had finished preaching the sutra, the devas, nāgas, spirits, the four heavenly kings, and their retinues, along with all the people of the world and the entire great assembly, paid homage to the Buddha and each departed for their own abodes.
The Sūtra on the Parinirvāṇa of King Śuddhodana Spoken by the Buddha.
